sections.title: 1. Types of Investment Risk — Systematic vs. Nonsystematic
sections.overview: All investment risk is classified as either systematic (market-wide, undiversifiable) or nonsystematic (issuer/industry-specific, diversifiable). The SIE expects candidates to identify each risk type, recognize which products are most exposed, and pair the risk with the appropriate mitigation technique.
key_concepts: Systematic risk = risk inherent to the entire market; cannot be eliminated by diversification within an asset class.
Market risk (price risk): the risk that the overall market declines, dragging down individual securities; chiefly an equity risk.
Interest-rate risk: risk that rising rates depress fixed-income prices; greatest for long-duration, low-coupon bonds.
Reinvestment risk: risk that coupon/principal proceeds must be reinvested at lower prevailing rates; the inverse of interest-rate risk; affects callable bonds and laddered portfolios.
Inflation (purchasing-power) risk: risk that real returns are eroded by inflation; greatest for fixed-rate long bonds and cash equivalents.
Currency (exchange-rate) risk: risk that foreign-currency-denominated assets lose value when the foreign currency weakens vs. USD; affects ADRs, foreign bonds, international funds.
Political/legislative/sovereign risk: risk of adverse government action, expropriation, tax-law change, or war; greatest in emerging markets.
Nonsystematic risk = risk specific to an issuer, industry, or sector; reducible through diversification.
Business risk: risk that an issuer's operations underperform (poor management, declining sales).
Financial (credit/default) risk: risk that the issuer cannot meet debt obligations; measured by credit rating.
Regulatory/legislative risk: risk that new rules harm a particular industry (e.g., utilities, pharma).
Liquidity (marketability) risk: risk of being unable to sell quickly at fair value; high in thinly-traded bonds, limited partnerships, private placements.
Call risk / prepayment risk: risk an issuer redeems debt early when rates fall, forcing reinvestment at lower yields; prepayment risk is the mortgage-backed analog.
Capital risk: risk of losing principal — present in all securities except direct U.S. Treasury obligations held to maturity.
Opportunity cost: forgone return from choosing one investment over another (risk-free rate is the benchmark).
rules: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) requires the registered rep to understand the risks of any recommended security before recommending it.
17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest) — Care Obligation requires the broker-dealer to understand the potential risks, rewards, and costs of a recommendation.
formulas: Total Risk = Systematic Risk + Nonsystematic Risk
Real Return ≈ Nominal Return − Inflation Rate
Risk Premium = Expected Return − Risk-Free Rate
mnemonics: Systematic risks — "PRIME": Purchasing-power (inflation), Reinvestment, Interest-rate, Market, Exchange-rate (currency). Add Political for sovereign exposure.
Nonsystematic risks — "ABCDL-R": (A)Business, (B)usiness/management, (C)redit (financial), (D)efault, (L)iquidity, (R)egulatory.
Systematic = "Same for all"; Nonsystematic = "Not for all."

sections.title: 2. Risk Mitigation Techniques
sections.overview: Different risks call for different defenses. Diversification addresses nonsystematic risk; asset allocation, hedging, and time horizon address systematic risk. Candidates must match technique to the specific exposure.
key_concepts: Diversification: spreading investments across issuers/industries/asset classes reduces nonsystematic risk; cannot eliminate systematic risk.
Asset allocation: strategic mix among stocks, bonds, cash, alternatives based on objectives and horizon; main defense against market risk.
Modern Portfolio Theory: combining negatively/low-correlated assets lowers portfolio standard deviation for a given expected return (efficient frontier).
Hedging: offsetting positions using options (protective puts, covered calls), futures, or inverse ETFs.
Laddering bonds: staggering maturities mitigates interest-rate and reinvestment risk by ensuring continuous reinvestment at varied rates.
Barbell strategy: short + long maturities; balances liquidity with yield.
Bullet strategy: maturities clustered at a target date; matches a future liability.
Dollar-cost averaging: investing fixed dollars at regular intervals lowers average cost per share over time; mitigates timing risk.
Buying TIPS or floating-rate notes mitigates inflation/interest-rate risk.
Buying investment-grade or insured (e.g., U.S. Treasuries, GOs) securities mitigates default risk.
Mitigating currency risk: currency-hedged funds, forward contracts, or holding domestic securities.
Mitigating liquidity risk: avoid thinly traded issues; hold listed securities and money-market reserves.
Time horizon: longer horizons absorb market volatility; shorter horizons demand higher-grade, shorter-duration holdings.
Beta measures systematic risk relative to the market (β = 1.0 = market; >1.0 more volatile; <1.0 less).
Standard deviation measures total volatility (total risk).
Alpha measures excess return vs. expected return given beta — manager skill.
rules: FINRA Rule 2111 requires that a recommended investment strategy (including portfolio construction and asset allocation) be in the customer's best interest based on the investment profile.
17 CFR 240.15l-1 Reg BI Care Obligation — the rep must have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation, including a series of recommendations, is in the retail customer's best interest.
formulas: Expected Return (two-asset) = Wa × Ra + Wb × Rb
Portfolio Beta = Σ (Weight_i × Beta_i)
Sharpe Ratio = (Rp − Rf) / σp
Alpha = Actual Return − [Rf + β × (Rm − Rf)]
mnemonics: "DAHL" — Diversify, Allocate, Hedge, Ladder.
Beta = systematic measure; Standard Deviation = total measure; Alpha = skill.

sections.title: 3. What Constitutes a Recommendation
sections.overview: Whether communication is a "recommendation" triggers suitability and Reg BI obligations. The determination is facts-and-circumstances based on whether a reasonable person would view the communication as a call to action for a specific security or strategy.
key_concepts: A recommendation = a communication that, viewed objectively, would reasonably be considered a call to action regarding a particular security or investment strategy involving securities.
Indicators of a recommendation: specificity, individual tailoring, frequency, and whether it suggests buying, selling, or holding.
Not recommendations (generally): general educational material, market commentary not tied to a specific security, asset-allocation models meeting safe-harbor criteria, and tools widely disseminated.
Solicited order: rep suggested the security — triggers suitability/Reg BI.
Unsolicited order: customer initiated — must be marked unsolicited on the order ticket; does not trigger Reg BI (but firm still has fair-dealing obligation).
Hold recommendations are explicitly covered by Reg BI and Rule 2111.
Implicit recommendations (e.g., reallocating a discretionary account) are also covered.
rules: FINRA Rule 2111 — Suitability applies to recommended transactions and investment strategies, including recommendations to hold.

17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Reg BI) — applies whenever a broker-dealer or associated person makes a recommendation of any securities transaction or investment strategy involving securities to a retail customer.
FINRA Rule 2010 — Standards of Commercial Honor and Just and Equitable Principles of Trade underlies fair dealing on all orders, solicited or not.
mnemonics: "Call-to-Action" test — if it tells the customer to DO something specific, it's a recommendation.

sections.title: 4. Reg BI — Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR 240.15l-1)
sections.overview: Reg BI is the federal conduct standard for broker-dealer recommendations to retail customers. Compliance was required by 6/30/2020. It is satisfied only by meeting four component obligations: Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance.
key_concepts: Applies when a BD or associated person makes a recommendation of a securities transaction or investment strategy to a retail customer.
Retail customer = a natural person (or legal rep) who receives a recommendation and uses it primarily for personal, family, or household purposes.

Disclosure Obligation: full and fair written disclosure, before/at time of recommendation, of material facts about the relationship, scope/type of services, fees, conflicts, and capacity (broker vs. adviser).

Care Obligation: rep must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to: (1) understand risks/rewards/costs, (2) have a reasonable basis the recommendation is in the retail customer's best interest, (3) avoid excessive trading regardless of discretion.

Conflict of Interest Obligation: written policies & procedures to identify and at minimum disclose, or eliminate, conflicts; eliminate sales contests, quotas, bonuses based on specific securities in a limited time.
Compliance Obligation: written P&Ps reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI as a whole.
Cannot satisfy Reg BI by disclosure alone — best-interest standard is substantive.
Reg BI does not apply to recommendations to institutional customers (FINRA Rule 2111 institutional-customer exemption may apply).
rules: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 — Regulation Best Interest; effective compliance date 6/30/2020.
17 CFR 240.17a-14 — Form CRS requirement for BDs (retail-investor relationship summary).
FINRA Rule 2111 — Suitability remains in effect; Reg BI supersedes Rule 2111 for retail recommendations but Rule 2111 still applies to institutional customers.
mnemonics: Reg BI's four obligations = "DC³" — Disclosure, Care, Conflict, Compliance.
Care Obligation sub-prongs = "RRC" — Reasonable basis (general), Recommendation-specific (this customer), Customer's series (no excessive trading).

sections.title: 5. Form CRS (Customer/Client Relationship Summary)
sections.overview: Form CRS is a short, plain-English disclosure delivered to retail investors describing the firm's relationship, services, fees, conflicts, and disciplinary history. Required of broker-dealers under 17 CFR 240.17a-14.
key_concepts: Delivered to a retail investor: at the earliest of (a) opening an account, (b) recommending a securities transaction or investment strategy, (c) recommending an account type or rollover, or (d) placing an order.
Maximum 2 pages (4 for dual registrants).
Must include prescribed "Conversation Starter" questions.
Filed with the SEC and posted on the firm's public website.
Updated within 30 days of becoming materially inaccurate, with communication of changes to existing customers within 60 days.
rules: 17 CFR 240.17a-14 — Form CRS preparation, filing, and delivery requirements for broker-dealers.
mnemonics: "CRS = Customer Relationship Summary" — short, plain-English, retail-only.

sections.title: 6. Know Your Customer & Customer Investment Profile
sections.overview: Suitable recommendations require firm knowledge of the customer. Rule 2090 (KYC) demands essential facts to service the account; Rule 2111 catalogs the investment profile elements forming the basis for any recommendation.
key_concepts: KYC essential facts (Rule 2090): facts needed to (a) effectively service the account, (b) act on instructions, (c) understand authority of any person acting for the customer, (d) comply with applicable laws and rules.

Customer investment profile elements (Rule 2111): age, other investments, financial situation and needs, tax status, investment objectives, investment experience, investment time horizon, liquidity needs, risk tolerance, and any other information the customer may disclose.
Customer objectives (rank by priority): preservation of capital, income, growth, growth & income, speculation, tax advantage, liquidity.
Time horizon: short-term (<3 yrs), intermediate (3–10 yrs), long-term (>10 yrs); drives risk capacity.
Risk tolerance: subjective willingness to bear loss; distinct from risk capacity (objective ability).
Tax status: marginal bracket determines attractiveness of municipal bonds (tax-equivalent yield) and tax-deferred vehicles.
rules: FINRA Rule 2090 — Know Your Customer; requires firms to use reasonable diligence to know essential facts about every customer.
FINRA Rule 2111 — Suitability; three main obligations: reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability.
FINRA Rule 4512 — Customer Account Information; lists information required to be obtained when opening an account.
formulas: Tax-Equivalent Yield = Municipal Yield / (1 − Marginal Tax Rate)
After-Tax Yield = Taxable Yield × (1 − Marginal Tax Rate)
mnemonics: Objectives priority — "PIGSTL": Preservation, Income, Growth, Speculation, Tax-advantage, Liquidity.
Profile elements — "FORT-ART": Financial situation, Objectives, Risk tolerance, Tax status, Age, Risk experience, Time horizon (plus liquidity, other investments).
KYC = "Know · Service · Act · Authority" (four pillars of Rule 2090).

sections.title: 7. Matching Customer Objectives to Investment Characteristics
sections.overview: Each product class has a risk/return profile suited to certain objectives. The SIE tests whether a candidate can match the right product to the stated objective and constraints.
key_concepts: Preservation of capital → U.S. Treasury bills/notes, money market funds, bank CDs, high-grade short bonds.
Current income (taxable account) → corporate bonds, preferred stock, REITs, bond funds, dividend-paying utilities.
Current income (high tax bracket) → municipal bonds (federally tax-exempt; in-state often state/local exempt).
Growth → common stock of growth companies, growth mutual funds, growth-oriented ETFs.
Growth & income → blue-chip dividend payers, balanced funds, equity-income funds.
Speculation/aggressive growth → small-cap, emerging-market equities, options, leveraged ETFs, sector funds.
Liquidity → money market instruments, listed equities, exchange-traded bonds; AVOID DPPs, hedge funds, illiquid bonds.
Inflation hedge → TIPS, equities (long-run), real assets/commodities, real estate.
Tax deferral → annuities (variable/fixed), qualified plans, IRAs.
Tax-free income → municipal bonds, Roth IRA qualified distributions.
Retirement savings → IRAs, 401(k)s, target-date funds; mix shifts to fixed income as horizon shortens.
Education funding → 529 plans, Coverdell ESAs, UTMA/UGMA.
DPPs are unsuitable for income/liquidity-focused investors — designed for high-net-worth investors seeking passive losses and long horizons.
rules: FINRA Rule 2111 — Customer-specific suitability requires the recommendation be suitable based on the customer's profile.
17 CFR 240.15l-1 — Reg BI Care Obligation requires the recommendation be in the retail customer's best interest in light of the profile.
formulas: After-Tax Yield (municipal vs. taxable comparison): see Section 6.
mnemonics: "Higher return = higher risk" — risk-return tradeoff is universal.
Retirement income clients = "safety + income" → bonds, dividend stocks, annuities; AVOID speculative options.

sections.title: 8. Major Market Benchmarks and Indices
sections.overview: Benchmarks measure market performance and serve as comparison standards for portfolios. Candidates must know weighting methodology, breadth, and what market segment each index represents.
key_concepts: DJIA (Dow Jones Industrial Average): 30 large-cap U.S. blue-chip stocks; PRICE-WEIGHTED (high-priced stocks have greater influence).
S&P 500: 500 large-cap U.S. stocks; MARKET-CAP-WEIGHTED (float-adjusted); the standard U.S. equity benchmark.
Nasdaq Composite: all common stocks listed on Nasdaq; market-cap-weighted; technology-heavy.
Nasdaq 100: 100 largest non-financial Nasdaq-listed companies.
Russell 2000: 2,000 small-cap U.S. stocks; primary small-cap benchmark; market-cap-weighted.
Russell 3000: broad U.S. market — largest 3,000 stocks (~98% of U.S. investable equity).
Wilshire 5000: total U.S. equity market index — broadest U.S. equity gauge.
MSCI EAFE: developed markets ex-U.S./Canada — Europe, Australasia, Far East; benchmark for international equity.
MSCI Emerging Markets Index: emerging-market equity benchmark.
Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index: broad U.S. investment-grade bond benchmark.
Other measures: NYSE Composite, Value Line (geometric, equal-weighted).
formulas: Price-Weighted Index Value = Σ Prices / Divisor   (DJIA methodology)
Market-Cap-Weighted Index Value ∝ Σ (Price × Shares Outstanding)   (S&P 500, Nasdaq, Russell methodology)
mnemonics: "DJIA = Dollar; S&P = Size" — Dow is price-weighted, S&P is cap-weighted.
Small-cap → Russell 2000; Total U.S. → Wilshire 5000; International developed → EAFE.

sections.title: 9. Quantitative Risk and Return Measures
sections.overview: The SIE expects familiarity with statistical measures used to describe and compare risk and return. These appear in performance reports, suitability discussions, and Reg BI cost-vs.-benefit analyses.
key_concepts: Standard deviation (σ): measures dispersion of returns; proxy for total risk (both systematic and nonsystematic).
Beta (β): measures sensitivity to overall market returns; systematic-risk measure. β=1 market; β>1 aggressive; β<1 defensive; β<0 inverse.
Alpha (α): risk-adjusted excess return vs. CAPM expected return — measures manager value-add.
Sharpe Ratio: excess return per unit of total risk (uses σ).
R-squared: % of a fund's movement explained by its benchmark (0–1.0); high R² makes beta meaningful.
Correlation coefficient (−1 to +1): combining low/negative correlations reduces portfolio risk.
Duration: bond price sensitivity to interest-rate changes; longer duration = greater interest-rate risk.
Total return = (income + capital gain/loss) / beginning value.
rules: FINRA Rule 2210 — Communications with the Public requires that performance figures and risk disclosures be fair, balanced, and not misleading.
formulas: Total Return = (Ending Value − Beginning Value + Income) / Beginning Value
Holding Period Return = (P1 − P0 + Distributions) / P0
Annualized Return ≈ (1 + Periodic Return)^n − 1
Sharpe Ratio = (Rp − Rf) / σp
CAPM: Expected Return = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf)
Portfolio σ depends on weights, individual σ, and correlations between assets.
mnemonics: "σ = Total · β = Market · α = Skill."
Higher Sharpe = better risk-adjusted return.

sections.title: 10. Suitability Obligations Under FINRA Rule 2111 (Institutional & Quantitative)
sections.overview: Rule 2111 contains three suitability obligations. Reg BI now governs retail recommendations, but Rule 2111 remains the SRO standard, especially for institutional customers, and supplies the quantitative-suitability framework.
key_concepts: Reasonable-basis suitability: the rep must have a reasonable basis to believe, after reasonable diligence, that the recommendation is suitable for AT LEAST SOME investors.
Customer-specific suitability: a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is suitable for THIS particular customer based on his/her investment profile.
Quantitative suitability: even individually suitable recommendations, when taken together, cannot be excessive (anti-churning) when the rep has actual or de facto control over the account.

Institutional-customer exemption: customer-specific suitability deemed satisfied if (a) the firm has reasonable basis to believe the institutional customer is capable of evaluating risks independently, and (b) the institutional customer affirmatively indicates it is exercising independent judgment.
Hold recommendations are covered.
Reg BI's Care Obligation effectively raises the standard from "suitable" to "in the best interest of" the retail customer.
rules: FINRA Rule 2111 — Suitability (three obligations).
FINRA Rule 2090 — Know Your Customer.
17 CFR 240.15l-1 — Reg BI (supersedes Rule 2111 for retail recommendations).
FINRA Rule 2010 — fair dealing principles.
formulas: Turnover Ratio = Total Annual Purchases / Average Monthly Equity   (excessive trading indicator)
Cost-to-Equity Ratio = Total Annual Costs / Average Equity   (break-even commission burden)
mnemonics: Suitability's three prongs = "R-C-Q": Reasonable-basis, Customer-specific, Quantitative.
Reg BI ≥ Rule 2111 — best interest is a HIGHER bar than mere suitability.

sections.title: 11. Putting It Together — The Recommendation Workflow
sections.overview: On exam scenarios, apply a consistent decision sequence: gather profile, identify objective, screen products by risk profile, select a best-interest recommendation, document, and disclose.
key_concepts: Step 1 — KYC (Rule 2090, Rule 4512): gather essential facts and profile data at account opening.
Step 2 — Identify primary objective and any constraints (time horizon, liquidity, taxes, risk tolerance).
Step 3 — Match product characteristics to objective; eliminate clearly unsuitable products.
Step 4 — Apply Reg BI Care Obligation: weigh risks, rewards, costs; reasonably available alternatives need not be exhaustively reviewed but must be considered.
Step 5 — Disclose material facts, fees, capacity, and conflicts (Reg BI Disclosure + Form CRS).
Step 6 — Document the basis for the recommendation; mark order solicited or unsolicited.
Step 7 — Supervisory review (Rule 3110); monitor for quantitative suitability over time.

Red flags requiring escalation: speculative recommendations to retirees seeking income, recommending illiquid products to clients with liquidity needs, recommending margin/options without experience, frequent trading in a small account, or recommendations producing high cost-to-equity ratios.
rules: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Reg BI).
17 CFR 240.17a-14 (Form CRS).
mnemonics: Workflow = "K-O-M-C-D-D-S": Know, Objective, Match, Care-test, Disclose, Document, Supervise.
